sections.h2: How does selling a house in Dayton, Ohio work?
sections.html:
A Dayton seller lists with an agent, sells without one, or accepts a cash purchase, and every path runs through a city disclosure step that most Ohio cities do not have. Dayton is the Montgomery County seat, founded in 1796 along the Great Miami River, and it is the sixth-most populous city in Ohio. The Census Bureau counted 137,644 residents in 2020 and estimates 136,688 for July 2025.

The city covers about 55.8 square miles of land. Dayton sits roughly 55 miles southwest of Columbus and 40 miles north of Cincinnati, which puts it in the middle of the Miami Valley.

sections.h2: What does Dayton's economy mean for people who own homes here?
sections.html:
The economy leans on aerospace, defense, health care and education, and each of those anchors affects neighborhoods in a different way. Wright-Patterson Air Force Base is nearby, and the Air Force Institute of Technology, the University of Dayton and Wright State University add research and student demand. Sinclair Community College is described as the largest community college at a single location in Ohio.

The city grew on canals, inventors and factories. The Dayton to Cincinnati canal began construction in 1827, and the Wright brothers developed their airplane here. Heavy manufacturing declined in the late twentieth century, and the city shifted toward services. Population peaked in the 1960 count at 262,332, so many Dayton blocks were built for a much larger city than the current one.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers show about housing in Dayton?
sections.html:
Dayton has the lowest home values and the highest renter share of the four cities in this group. These are the Census Bureau's QuickFacts figures for 2020 through 2024.

  • Median value of owner-occupied housing: $100,600.
  • Owner-occupied rate: 48.4 percent, so just over half of households rent.
  • Households: 58,477, averaging 2.12 people each.
  • Median gross rent: $918; median owner cost with a mortgage: $1,147.
  • Median household income: $45,247; mean commute 20.3 minutes.

With so many renters, a lot of Dayton houses are sold by landlords with tenants still inside, and many others come from estates. Both situations are covered further down.

sections.h2: Which Dayton neighborhoods carry the most history?
sections.html:
Ten historic neighborhoods are called out for mostly single-family houses and mansions: Oregon District, Wright Dunbar, Dayton View, Grafton Hill, McPherson Town, Webster Station, Huffman, Kenilworth, St. Anne's Hill and South Park. Their architecture runs through Queen Anne, Craftsman, Tudor Revival, Colonial Revival, American Foursquare and several other styles. Downtown Dayton is a separate large area made up of several neighborhoods.

A seller in one of these areas should expect buyers to ask about original windows, roof age and any past repairs. The suburbs around the city include Kettering, Beavercreek, Centerville, Huber Heights, Miamisburg and Oakwood, among others with populations above 10,000, and many Dayton buyers compare listings across those lines.

sections.h2: What is the City of Dayton property disclosure and when is it required?
sections.html:
Any sale of a property inside the city requires a Certificate of Disclosure that tells the buyer about open housing code violations. The city says to look at the parcel number: if it starts with R72 or R726, the property is in Dayton and the form must be filed. The form exists to inform the buyer, and the city's FAQ says it is not meant to stop a sale.

  • With no open violations, the seller signs and supplies the buyer's contact details.
  • With open violations, the form must show the violation or structural nuisance status, a flat $60 fee is paid (not per violation), and both parties sign, with the buyer's signature notarized.
  • The buyer agrees either that the violations are corrected before the sale or that the buyer will make the listed repairs within 90 days.
  • The title company usually asks the city for violation information and pending bills 7 to 10 business days before closing.

The city also states plainly that selling a property in Dayton does not remove its violations. They transfer with the house.

sections.h2: Who handles code violations and nuisance properties in Dayton?
sections.html:
The Division of Housing and Inspections enforces the housing ordinance and the public nuisance ordinance. Its remit also covers trees and trash, non-residential exterior maintenance, and abandoned or junk vehicles. For an open violation notice or citation, call 937-333-3867 or 937-333-8645.

Two online tools help a seller see what a buyer can see. The Dayton Housing Tracker searches by address or neighborhood, and the Dayton Housing Condition Survey portal lets users review housing conditions by neighborhood. Complaints and service requests go through Dayton Delivers. Looking up your own address before listing shows whether a citation is on file.

sections.h2: How does Dayton weather affect a house sale?
sections.html:
Dayton has hot, humid summers and cold winters, with about 41 inches of precipitation and roughly 23 inches of snow in a normal year. Severe thunderstorms, floods, blizzards and tornadoes are all possible. On Memorial Day 2019, a tornado outbreak put 15 tornadoes on the ground in the Dayton area, including an EF4 that tore through Brookville, Trotwood, Dayton, Northridge and Riverside.

Roofs, siding and basements are the usual places buyers look for storm history. Keep repair invoices, insurance claim paperwork and contractor names together so you can answer questions on the Ohio disclosure form with documents instead of memory.

sections.h2: What should a Dayton landlord know before selling a rental?
sections.html:
A landlord selling a rental should check city permit rules, tenant protections and short-term use before setting a price. Dayton requires a contractor registered with the city for plumbing, electrical and HVAC work on rental property, on an unoccupied house that will be rented, and on duplexes, even where the owner lives in one half. Owner-occupants may do some of that work themselves after getting the right permits.

The city's FAQ also describes source of income rules: landlords cannot refuse a prospective tenant because rent comes from vouchers, subsidies, benefits or other public assistance. For short-term rentals, the city defines them as stays under 30 consecutive days and says it has no registration system, handling concerns case by case. Ask the city planning office what applies before you sell to a buyer planning to use the house that way.

sections.h2: What does Montgomery County charge to transfer a deed?
sections.html:
The Montgomery County Auditor handles the deed transfer, and the Recorder records the deed afterward. The county's pages post the rates below.

Montgomery County deed transfer and recording rates (source: county Deed Transfer page and Recorder FAQ)
StepRate as posted
Conveyance fee$3 per $1,000 of the actual sale price
Per parcel$.50 for each parcel transferred
Recording a deed$34 for the first two pages, $8 per additional page
Payment to the RecorderCash, check or money order to the Montgomery County Recorder

The deed must go to the Auditor's Deed Transfer Department for a transfer stamp before it reaches the Recorder. For questions, the Auditor's deed transfer line is 937-225-4373. Electronic filing is available through two named e-recording services.

sections.h2: What does Ohio law require on top of the city form?
sections.html:
Separately, state law (R.C. 5302.30) has the seller of a one-to-four-unit home fill out Ohio's own condition form and deliver a signed copy. If the buyer sees it only after a contract is signed, a written cancellation is allowed for three business days after receipt, ending no later than thirty days from acceptance or closing, whichever is first.

The state form does not replace Dayton's own certificate. A seller needs both, and the city's certificate concerns open code violations rather than the physical condition items the state form covers.

faqs.q: How do I know if my Dayton property needs the city disclosure?
faqs.a: Check the parcel number. A number beginning with R72 or R726 is inside the City of Dayton and requires a Certificate of Disclosure, with exceptions for three types of transfer listed on the city's FAQ.

faqs.q: What does an open violation cost me at sale?
faqs.a: The city charges a flat $60 fee with the disclosure form when there is an open violation, not a per-violation fee. The buyer must also sign before a notary and agree to corrections within 90 days or earlier repairs.

faqs.q: Does selling a Dayton house clear its code violations?
faqs.a: No. The city states that a transfer or sale does not remove violations from a property, so they pass to the buyer, who has agreed to resolve them.

faqs.q: What is the Montgomery County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The county's Deed Transfer page lists a mandatory conveyance fee of $3 per $1,000 of the actual sale price plus $.50 for each parcel transferred.
The city's FAQ says it has no system to register or regulate short-term rentals and handles concerns case by case. It defines a short-term rental as a stay of less than 30 consecutive days.
